title: School Structure & Policy: Looping
author: Teach Beyond Borders
summary: This post makes the case for looping, where a teacher moves up a grade with the same class, as a cheap answer to what it calls the September tax of starting over every year. It defines the practice, distinguishing it from retention and multiage classrooms, and then reviews repeat-teacher studies from North Carolina, Tennessee and Chile that find modest gains in scores, attendance and behaviour. The author is candid that effects are small, that most studies capture accidental rather than planned repeat matches, and that planned looping may do better or worse. The mechanisms offered are time saved on getting to know students, deeper trust and stronger family relationships. A frank list of costs follows: bad matches last twice as long, teachers must know two curricula, newcomers enter closed groups, labels can stick and staffing turnover breaks loops. The close suggests teachers and parents explore partial looping and frames schools as running on relationships that take time.
points: Looping removes the 'September tax' by keeping teacher knowledge of students from walking out the door each June.
Studies in North Carolina, Tennessee and Chile find modest gains of 0.02 to 0.12 standard deviations, with benefits in attendance and behaviour too.
Most evidence comes from accidental repeat matches, so the effect of deliberate looping programmes remains unknown.
The gains are attributed to time, trust and family relationships rather than any special technique.
The costs are real, including doubled bad matches, double curriculum prep, closed peer groups and fragile staffing, so opt-outs and monitoring matter.
quotes: Then June comes, and all that knowledge walks out the door. The next teacher starts from zero. So does the kid.
Most of these studies measure kids who happened to get the same teacher again, not formal looping programs.

What does 0.02 to 0.12 standard deviations mean? It’s modest. Nobody’s life is transformed by one looped year. But most education reforms cost millions and deliver less. This one mostly costs a scheduling decision.
In a looped room, the first day of year two looks a lot like the last day of year one. Routines are set.
The teacher already knows whose essays stall at the thesis and who needs the directions read twice. Instruction starts in week one, not week six.
A bad match lasts twice as long. Every teacher has had a kid they never quite reached. Looping without an exit ramp turns one hard year into two.
Looping is a tool, not a fix, and it works best when someone is watching who it’s working for.
We talk about schools as places that deliver content, and we argue endlessly about which content. Looping is a reminder that schools also run on relationships, and relationships take time.
